 Checking food safety at NKU in an era of recalls
 Rebecca Taylor , News editor 
 November 2, 2026 
 Corey G. Zimmerman 
 Food recall notifications have become a lock screen regular lately. 
 The number of recalls, though, is closer to steady than surging. The FDA and USDA classified approximately 215 food recall events between Jan. 1 and Sept. 31, comparable to the pace in the same period last year, according to an examination of the agency’s published reports.
 The alerts also land close to home. Kentucky was named in the distribution of 45 of those recalls, though a state listing means a product was distributed there, not necessarily that it reached NKU or the surrounding area.
 Keeping a recalled product off the serving line is the responsibility of Chartwells, the food service company that has run NKU dining since 2005 . NKU’s food policy puts nearly all campus food service under Chartwells, making it the university’s exclusive provider, with only limited exceptions such as athletics concessions and residence hall kitchens.
 For the several hundred students who eat on NKU’s campus each day, those processes and policies happen behind the counter, or even before the food makes it to the kitchen.
 The first line of defense is traceability. Chartwells says it only approves vendors that can track potentially affected products through item numbers and purchasing records. The company’s “Red Alert” system, which sends concise summaries containing information on recalls and product safety alerts, immediately notifies all locations that have a possibility of being affected.
 Chartwells also requires a ServSafe-certified position officially known as a Person in Charge on every shift. ServSafe is a food safety program created by the National Restaurant Association. According to ServSafe, its training and certification program is recognized by more federal, state and local jurisdictions than any other food safety credential.
 ServSafe certification is valid for five years, but Chartwells renews its managers’ certifications every three years. The shorter cycle is meant to keep managers current on practices and regulations.
 Jada Kidd, a junior who has worked in NKU Dining for three years, said of the arrangement between NKU and Chartwells, “It’s like [my supervisors] work under Chartwells, but [they] also work under NKU.”
 “If any big change happens, it’s Chartwells. But if it’s a minor thing for students, like schedules, it’s NKU. It’s, like, a joint custody,” Kidd said.
 Kidd said the pre-shift meetings are where new concerns reach the line workers. These meetings also give student workers a chance to ask questions about new recalls, updates and precautions.
 © 2026 Corey G. Zimmerman 
 Chartwells says all dining associates participate in annual food allergy training as part of their ongoing food safety education. Since undeclared allergens are a common culprit of recalls, annual allergy training is especially relevant. Undeclared allergens have been the top 2026 food-recall hazard, according to Recall Bench , a website that aggregates public-domain recall data from multiple U.S. government agencies.
 Allergen information is made visible to diners in Norse Commons with signage above the food listing each dish’s name as well as dietary descriptors like whether it is vegetarian, vegan or gluten-free.
 “[We use] completely separate utensils for all of our gluten-free things,” Kidd said. Norse Commons dining hall also recently got a gluten-free waffle maker, which it keeps apart from the regular one.
 Staff must also keep production and receiving logs, along with refrigeration and freezer temperature records. On top of those, Chartwells also structures its review process with daily food safety checks, monthly food safety walkthroughs and quarterly food safety assessments. The quarterly reviews examine “sanitation, labeling, safe receiving practices, time and temperature controls and regulatory compliance,” Chatwells said in a statement to The Northerner .
 Health inspectors typically visit around lunchtime, Kidd said. They check that everything in the walk-in refrigerator and freezer is labeled and dated, and they examine equipment such as the drink machines.
 Northern Kentucky Health Department records show 10 of 13 listed NKU food locations with a perfect 100 on their most recent inspection. Einstein Brothers Bagels scored 99 on Sept. 8, and FUEL NKU scored 98 in February. Norse Commons Cafeteria initially scored 95 on May 7, then 100 on a follow-up inspection 12 days later.
 Kidd said she has seen little change in food safety practices in recent years, though workers have become “more cautious” amid the national reports of foodborne illness. Salmonella, for example, was the reason for 47 of this year’s FDA list of food recalls.
 Food safety at NKU is not limited to the dining halls. FUEL NKU, the university’s on-campus food pantry , is one of the few food-related operations on campus that is outside of Chartwells. It faces its own challenge regarding food safety. Staff say they handle it with hands-on inspection and a chain of donors that also act as an early-warning system.
 Because the product passes through several sources, each one has a chance to weed out potential problems. The pantry buys some of its product from Master Provisions and the Freestore Foodbank. It also receives donations from groups like La Soupe. Last Mile Food Rescue also brings in items from retailers such as Kroger, Publix and sometimes Walmart.
 Nick Bliven, program coordinator for FUEL NKU, said the pantry often ends up “the second, secondhand” recipient of food, so everything gets checked before it goes out.
 “We’re always inspecting food before it goes out — [check] if [packaging is] open, or visually looking at it, or if it has an odor,” Bliven said. Staff look for blemishes and mold, then compost what they discard.
 They train student employees with a simple test: “Would you eat this?”
 Some items never make it to the shelf. The pantry does not accept anything damaged or open, and it turns away produce from home gardens.
 “One person brought tomatoes, and I’m like, unfortunately, [we] can’t get those out to people,” Bliven said.
 Peg Adams, director of FUEL NKU, said staff had been trained on food safety protocols and procedures. “We’ve been certified through the Northern Kentucky Health Department, and so through those classes and certification, we’ve learned a lot about food safety.”
 Employees are also trained in first-in, first-out storage, labeling boxes with dates so older goods go out first.
 “We’ve worked with our employees to make sure that when goods come in, especially non-perishables, that we label the boxes with the dates and we store them appropriately so that we have easier access to the goods that need to be used first, and so we circulate things that way,” Adams said.
 The pantry treats date labels as a teaching moment. “‘Best used by’ does not necessarily mean that it’s bad after that date,” Bliven said. “It’s more for quality.”
 Bliven added that the pantry does have a list to make sure that all workers know how long items can be kept past their dates while still ensuring quality and safety.
 Because the pantry is “seen as retail,” according to Bliven, it does not prepare food and instead hands it out “like you would in a convenience store.” If a retail donor issued a warning, both Adams and Bliven say FUEL NKU would immediately act on it.
 “Say we have lettuce from Publix, for example,” Bliven said. “If we received a message that said all lettuce at Publix is to be discarded, we would discard it and move forward from there. So we try to take a proactive approach.”
 When the cyclospora outbreak made headlines this past summer, the pantry was able to assure people: “This [lettuce] is safe. We promise.”
 “The lettuce that we had was [from] hydroponics.” Bliven said the lettuce was from 80 Acres Farms, a vertical farming company local to Hamilton, Ohio that has since announced its closure.
 Hydroponically grown produce has a lesser risk of contamination because it bypasses environmental factors like open fields and agricultural water, the main sources of the diarrhea-causing parasite, according to the FDA.
 “It was kind of ironic,” Blevin said.
 Adams said FUEL NKU’s goal is to give students something they can rely on. “We think it’s important that students have opportunities to work on their studies and focus on their academics, and not have to worry about where their next meal is going to come from,” she said.
 Adams added that food safety is also a shared responsibility at the consumer level. “Does it look right? Smell right? Are we washing our fruits and vegetables? Whether you’re shopping at a pantry or a grocery store or at a farmer’s market, these things are important to do for our own health.”
